Question_text: A sky-diver jumps from a stationary balloon. His initial downwards acceleration is 10m/s². Fig. 1.1 shows the directions of the air resistance and the weight of the sky-diver. The mass of the sky-diver is 60kg and his weight is 600N.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a diagram of a sky-diver falling. An upward arrow labelled 'air resistance' points from the sky-diver's body upwards. A downward arrow labelled 'weight' points from the sky-diver's center downwards.

Parts.part_text: Explain, using ideas about the forces, why his initial downwards acceleration is 10m/s².
When the parachute opens, the sky-diver experiences an upward acceleration for a short time. Explain why.

The total force of air resistance on the sky-diver and open parachute changes with their speed, as shown in Fig. 1.2. After the parachute opens, the sky-diver slows down to a terminal velocity. The weight of the sky-diver is 600N.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 shows a graph of air resistance (N) versus speed (m/s). The x-axis is speed from 0 to 6 m/s. The y-axis is air resistance from 0 to 800 N. The graph shows an upward curving line starting from (0,0) and reaching approximately (6, 750), indicating that air resistance increases with speed. The line shows a non-linear relationship where air resistance increases significantly with higher speeds.

Parts.part_text: Using Fig. 1.2, determine the terminal velocity of the sky-diver.
Calculate the resultant force on the sky-diver when his speed is 5.5m/s.

Question_text: A student hangs various masses from the end of a spring and determines the extension produced. Fig. 2.1 shows the spring hanging vertically on its own and with an unknown mass X at one end.
image: Fig. 2.1 shows two diagrams of a spring. The first diagram shows a spring hanging vertically, with its unextended length indicated as 10 cm. The second diagram shows the same spring hanging vertically with an unknown mass 'X' attached to its end, and its extended length indicated as 30 cm.

Parts.part_text: The student plots a graph of the extension of the spring against the mass hanging on the spring. Fig. 2.2 shows the student's graph.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.2 shows a graph of extension/cm versus mass/g. The x-axis (mass/g) ranges from 0 to 500. The y-axis (extension/cm) ranges from 0 to 40. The graph shows a straight line originating from (0,0) up to a point P, which is around (320g, 32cm), after which the line curves upwards, indicating a non-linear extension beyond this point.

Parts.part_text: At point P on the graph, the line begins to curve. State the name of point P.
Using Fig. 2.1 and Fig. 2.2, determine the mass X.
The gravitational field strength g is 10N/kg. Calculate the weight of X.
An identical spring is used with the original spring, as shown in Fig. 2.3. Together they support the mass X. State and explain how the extension in Fig. 2.3 compares with the extension in Fig. 2.1.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.3 shows two identical springs connected in parallel, both hanging vertically and supporting the mass X from below.

Question_text: Fig. 3.1 shows a thin sheet of plastic. A student tries to measure the thickness of the sheet with a ruler, but the sheet is too thin to measure accurately. The student measures the mass of the sheet and obtains the value 0.12 g.
image: Fig. 3.1 shows a perspective drawing of a thin rectangular sheet of plastic, indicating its general shape but no specific dimensions.

Parts.part_text: State what is meant by mass.

The student measures the length and width of the sheet. The readings obtained are: length of sheet = 3.0 cm, width of sheet = 2.0 cm. Calculate the thickness of the sheet.
State a measuring instrument that can be used to measure the thickness of the sheet accurately.

Parts.part_text: Draw a line from each box on the left-hand side to show which expands the most and which expands the least. Left boxes: 'expands the most', 'expands the least'. Right boxes: 'air', 'copper', 'water'.
Fig. 4.1 shows a mercury thermometer. This thermometer has a suitable range for use in laboratory experiments, but has a low sensitivity for some experiments.

With reference to this thermometer, describe what is meant by low sensitivity.
State one change in the design of a thermometer that increases its sensitivity.

The row for 'light' is partially filled: 'direction of vibration: perpendicular to the direction of transfer of the energy', 'type of wave: transverse'.

Parts.image: Fig. 5.2 shows a graph of height/m versus time/s, representing a wave's oscillation. The x-axis (time/s) ranges from 0 to 3.5. The y-axis (height/m) ranges from 0.70 to 1.30. Question_text: Explain what is meant by critical angle.

Calculate the refractive index of diamond.

Question_text: Fig. 7.1 shows part of a loudspeaker. A coil is attached to a paper cone and is suspended freely within a cylindrical magnet.

Question_text: Fig. 8.1 shows a circuit that contains a battery, a fixed resistor of resistance 1000Ω and a variable resistor R.
image: Fig. 8.1 shows a series electrical circuit diagram. A battery is connected in series with a fixed resistor of 1000 Ω and a variable resistor R.

Question_text: The circuit diagram shown in Fig. 9.2 uses an LDR as the sensor in an automatic night light. When it gets dark, the lamp turns on.

The temperature of a liquid is between its melting point and its boiling point. Using ideas about molecules, describe the changes that occur when the liquid evaporates.

Calculate the mass of nitrogen that boils away.

Question_text: The overall stopping distance of a cyclist is made up of two parts, as shown in Fig. 12.1: the distance the cyclist travels during the reaction time of the cyclist (the thinking distance), the distance the cyclist travels after the brakes are applied (the braking distance).
image: Fig. 12.1 shows a diagram illustrating the stopping distance of a cyclist. A cyclist on a bicycle is depicted. Arrows indicate 'thinking distance' and 'braking distance' contributing to the 'overall stopping distance'.

Parts.part_text: State the energy change that occurs during braking.
A ball rolls in front of a cyclist at time t = 0 and the cyclist brakes and comes to rest. Fig. 12.2 shows the speed-time graph for the cyclist.
Parts.image: Fig. 12.2 shows a speed-time graph for a cyclist. The x-axis (time/s) ranges from 0 to 2.4. The y-axis (speed/m/s) ranges from 0 to 8. The graph shows an initial constant speed of approximately 7.2 m/s from t=0 to t=0.4 s, followed by a linear decrease in speed until it reaches 0 m/s at t=2.4 s.

Parts.part_text: Using Fig. 12.2, determine the reaction time of the cyclist.
Using Fig. 12.2, calculate the thinking distance.
State how the braking distance is found using Fig. 12.2.

On another occasion, the same cyclist travels at an initial speed of 5.0m/s. A ball rolls in front of the cycle at time t = 0. The cyclist has the same reaction time and the deceleration of the cycle is the same as in Fig. 12.2. On Fig. 12.2 draw the new speed-time graph for the cyclist.
The braking distance is longer when the cyclist stops on a wet road. Explain why.
Fig. 12.3 shows the hydraulic braking system of the cycle.
Parts.image: Fig. 12.3 shows a diagram of a hydraulic braking system for a bicycle. It includes a brake lever connected to a pivot, which applies a force 'F' to a piston 'R' via a handlebar. Piston R is connected via oil in a hydraulic line to piston S, which in turn actuates brake pads against a spinning brake disc on the axle of a wheel.

Parts.part_text: The cyclist applies a force on the brake lever. This increases the pressure in the oil by 1.2 x 10⁶ Pa. The cross-sectional area of piston R is 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m². Calculate the force F applied by the brake lever to piston R.
The force applied to each of the brake pads is larger than F. Explain why.
